# Benchmarks

<!-- Generated by `just bench-docs` at the root of the repository; don't edit by hand. -->

phlite's Python bindings against reference implementations (with [pytest-benchmark](https://pytest-benchmark.readthedocs.io/)), and the Rust reduction on its own (with [criterion](https://bheisler.github.io/criterion.rs/book/)), on one machine.
In the Python tables each time is the fastest of several runs (one run for the largest cases), with the peak heap memory allocated during a separate run in MB (measured with [memray](https://bloomberg.github.io/memray/), which includes native allocations, such as Rust's). Parallel implementations use 4 threads. Every barcode agrees with the reference implementation's (each benchmark checks this).

* Machine: 11th Gen Intel(R) Core(TM) i7-1185G7 @ 3.00GHz (8 cores), Linux x86_64
* Measured 2026-11-12 at commit `aa991f3 (with uncommitted changes)`

Full results are in `python-tests/benchmarks/results/` (pytest-benchmark JSON; compare runs with `pytest-benchmark compare`). See [python-tests/README.md](README.md#benchmarks) for how to run them and check for regressions.

## Rips: `phlite_rips` vs ripser and giotto-ph

Vietoris–Rips persistence in dimensions up to `dim` of `n` points uniformly in the unit cube, from a distance matrix. giotto-ph is ripser with parallelism. The 1000- and 2000-point cases are timed once each, and at 1000 points in dimension 2 ripser runs out of memory (over 7 GB), so isn't run.

## GrPPH: `phlite_grpph` vs grpphati

Grounded persistent path homology (dimension 1) of random digraphs on `n` nodes, each edge present with probability `p`, with integer weights 1–5. `GrPPH_par_wedge` is grpphati's parallel pipeline over wedge components. The 200-node case is timed once each, and only phlite runs on it (grpphati needs over 5 GB at 100 nodes); its barcodes are checked against phlite's default.

## Sparse matrices: `phlite` vs PHAT and LoPHAT

Persistence of explicit boundary matrices over Z/2, given to every implementation as the same list of columns in filtration order. Times include loading the columns from Python, except for `(reduce)`, where the matrix is built before the clock starts. phlite's default stores the reduced columns of R and reduces with a dense pivot column (`pivot`, as PHAT does), without caching columns of D; other configurations are named by how they differ, and `V only` recomputes the columns of R from V instead. Larger cases are timed once each. `rips`: Rips complexes of `n` random points in the plane, up to triangles. `grid`: cubical complexes of `n`×`n` grids, filtered by smoothed noise on the vertices. `cells`: sparse random cellular complexes with `n` cells in each dimension up to 3. `dense`: the same, with dense boundaries.

Python 3.13.13.

## Rust: the clearing reduction

The core reduction alone, from criterion (`cargo bench`), on the Rips coboundary matrix of random points in the unit cube (`phlite_rips/benches/reduction.rs`) and the GrPPH coboundary matrix of random digraphs (`phlite_grpph/benches/reduction.rs`). Median time per reduction; `parallel …/N` uses N threads.
